Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling mysteries the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one aboard, if a man was found wandering around London in a space-suit, if the passenger of a Rolls Royce suddenly transmogrified into a skeleton, if a train pulling into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, you called on 'Department S' to sort things out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose fertile imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off show. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's show, the department was headed by a black man - 'Sir Curtis Seretse' ( Dennis Alaba Peters ) If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', it was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers & Partners, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many I.T.C. series, the music was composed by Edwin Astley. His theme for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best television themes of all time. Predictably, the show looks a little sexist and dated now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid of 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you've got 'Department S'! Steered text
Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller about a special team of detectives from Interpol, based in Geneva, sent to solve baffling crimes the police couldn't crack. If a plane arrived at an airport with no-one aboard, if a man was found walking around London in a space-suit, if the driver of a Rolls Royce was mysteriously turned into a skeleton or if a train pulling into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, it fell to 'Department S' to sort it out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', the team's psychologist, a crime novelist whose analytical mind helped crack many of the toughest cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later given a spin-off series. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart King' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the feisty 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's series, the team was led by a black man - 'Chiefi Seretse' played by Alaba Peters. If the show looked a bit like 'The Benny Hill Show', it was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors. The colourful titles, designed by Chambers & Partners, would be worth tuning in for alone. As for the music, so glad I didn to of that, the score was composed by Edwin Bing. His theme for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best television themes of all time. Predictably, the show was a little long and wordy, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine the best of 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' series and you've got 'Department S'! Fun Fact: The episode 'A Cold War of Nerves' features a young Sir Anthony Hopkins in a small role

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

Another fine entry in the Crime Doctor series [#9/10]. An atmospheric almost noirish black and white film with a splendid Spanish setting, a good supporting cast and a rather off-the-wall plot too. A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in his drawing room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a witness) and immediately and resignedly declares it murder. We are presented with a quite weird set of suspects to mull over, with one of them being the Doctor. There's the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the screaming brother of the dead 2nd wife, the dancing brother and his vampires, the handsome young man, the old cabinet maker, Corrigan on wheels, Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds and ends Cowan. Emory as the Doctor had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as the Doctor was a fine actor, with whom he was working at all times. One of the goofs listed in the credits is this: when called into the drawing room Ordway says "go through the centre of the room" and Cowan replies "I took the door this time". Good bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling for club music and beer at a nightclub to make up for their interrupted dinner party and the scene where Mrs Braga's place of abode is being rumbled. The plot does seem to be a bit slow at times and the way it was all wrapped up is perhaps not worthy of the series, but then it's the Crime Doctor and not Sherlock Holmes either! Well worth a watch for those already into the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you're a fan of the series.

All I can say after watching the DVDs of the first season is that I can not believe it was green-lighted for this long. It's a different kind of show, but it is worth it. For those who enjoyed the X-Files, we have a worthy successor. Not as mysterious or dark as Lost, I found it to be a perfect ride. This kind of extended story is hard to make. Most of them just degenerate into endless dribble and most of the elements do not work well together. In this case they do and I think the cast is great, the writing good, the location and production first rate, and the special effects very good for a television budget. What it is about is plausible, but as a story it is not so simple as to insult your intelligence. Bottomline is that this is great Sci-Fi entertainment for the entire family. I doubt it will be a classic with a long run like X-Files, but in the meantime well worth getting on DVD if you missed it like I did the first time around. This year my Sci-Fi collection has been increased by one great series. PS. I can't believe this was not on NBC...they must have some better picks..

Young Johnson and Carey, Jr. come across real well, but it is Bond's film to shine and he gives the best performance. Bond is the one who seems to know the most about the ways of the Mormonons and will certainly come in handy when certain things might happen as the two young boys ride along with them a bit. I'd have to say this is one of the best and most least known westerns and seems to hold up well.

Another story line describes these same issues from a different perspective in Pakistan, and another follows a struggling smuggler in Amsterdam and his relationship with a successful Hamburg smuggler. The fourth main storyline is the prosecution of a Hamburg smuggler and the conflicting perspectives of his wife and his lawyer, while he is on trial. It is an even greater accomplishment that a story that spans three countries and over a dozen main characters can be so clear and enthralling, never having to oversimplify. Martin Ritt's first film offers an exceptional existentialist answer (three years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who inadvertently disguised Kazan's offensive theme of trying to justify naming names (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and an upstart Sidney Poitier daring to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although the quite appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic, the courageous struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and violence has hardly aged at all. One wonders how shocked initial 1957 moviegoers were at such a bold presentation of white-black relations (if some of the bigoted didn't leave the theater early, they must of left dumbfounded, if not offended). The last reel of the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most jaded viewers will not realize what a radical and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. What's most disturbing about this lost classic: how it sadly remains unavailable on any format, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school or college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever at all.

Steered text
Martin Ritt's first film offers an interesting and timely alternative (three years prior) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" was immensely successful and led by Marlon Brando, who was a member of an American Communist close enough to justify naming him (at least in the eyes of the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Poitier and an upstart Sidney Lumet who dared to tackle issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although its very appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic today, his struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and classism has aged remarkably well. One wonders how the initial reception was, as many moviegoers were shocked by the frank presentation of anti-black prejudice (at least, the few who didn't leave the theater in a huff were left with their questions, if not disturbed). The final reel of the film is a surprise delight, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, a kind that tainted "Waterfront." Even the most jaded viewers will quickly realize what a powerful and important film "Edge of the City" ends up being. The most unfortunate thing about this lost classic is that it is not available on any DVD, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school and college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever..

Steered text
The Three Stooges have always been some of the funniest actors that I have loved. I have just about every one of the shorts that they have made. I love all six of the stooges (Curly, Shemp, Moe, Larry, Joe, and Curly Joe)! All of their shorts are hilarious and they have many other great actors (there are a lot of them) in many of their shorts. In this short, Jack Blackmer, is some of my favorite actors. He is the all time funniest actor and this short is one of the most hilarious Three Stooges shorts. Besides Jack Blackmer, this short has Bud Jamison, Jeanie Roberts, Phyllis Crane, Dell Henderson, Jr, Billy Bletcher, Billy Gilbert, and John Hiatt The acting by these actors is great especially by Jamison and Roberts. There are many funny scenes here that I think all Three Stooges fans will love. In my opinion this one of the most different Three Stooges shorts. I recommend this short to everyone

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this still does fine. Director Michael Davis even manages one or two creepy scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

Steered text
I got Monster Man in a box set of horror films where I mainly skipped the other titles, but had a very good time with this. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the good performances of Eric Jungman as the bumbling lead, Josh B. Jackson as a sarcastic friend and Aimee Song as the love interest. The plot is a bit predictable, borrowing from a number of other films, but is funny throughout, with a bit of gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this one does work. Director Michael Bay also manages one or two creepy moments, such as when the lead is in in jail. The acting is pretty good throughout if a bit messily cut and edited and for me, the film suffers a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title appears to be a fan of Slipknot and the film seems to go more for style but less for twisted and convincing horror. The final twist is a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of real suspense and overall messiness, this is a good example of unpretentious and often funny horror splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.
